subproblem.title: Multiplicity one makes the IM measure dominated by Hⁿ
subproblem.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ, U ⊆ ℝᴾ any set, and R = (M, θ, ξ_R) an integer multiplicity triple in U (IMRep U n) with μ := R.measure = (Hⁿ⌞M).withDensity θ, where Hⁿ = μHE[n] and θ = R.mult. Let B ⊆ ℝᴾ be measurable, and assume θ(x) = R.mult x = 1 for μ-a.e. x ∈ B. Then μ⌞B ≤ Hⁿ⌞B as measures (R.measure.restrict B ≤ μHE[n].restrict B). Moreover, for every set A ⊆ B and every function h : ℝᴾ → [0, ∞] (no measurability assumed), ∫⁻_A h dμ ≤ ∫⁻_A h dHⁿ (lower Lebesgue integrals over the restricted measures).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (U : Set (Euclid P)) (R : IMRep U n) (B : Set (Euclid P)), MeasurableSet B → (∀ᵐ x ∂R.measure, x ∈ B → R.mult x = 1) → R.measure.restrict B ≤ (μHE[n] : Measure (Euclid P)).restrict B ∧ ∀ (A : Set (Euclid P)) (h : Euclid P → ℝ≥0∞), A ⊆ B → (∫⁻ x in A, h x ∂R.measure) ≤ ∫⁻ x in A, h x ∂μHE[n]
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Step 5 of the parent proof of dorag_tes_graph_affine_height. It formalizes the passage in Simon, Ch. 5, proof of Theorem 4.5, book/chapter-05.txt lines 963–970, from the Hⁿ-integral over B_{θρ}(τ) ∩ graph f to the μ-integral over B_{θρ}(τ); the multiplicity is controlled at line 967. It is stated here for a general measurable set B and an arbitrary ambient dimension P. That step says: N := {x ∈ M ∩ B : θ(x) ≠ 1} has μ(N) = 0, and θ ≥ 1 on M, so Hⁿ(N) ≤ ∫_N θ dHⁿ = μ(N) = 0. Hence ∫_{S'} h dμ ≤ ∫_{S'} h dHⁿ for S' ⊆ B.
1. (Data.) θ : x ↦ (R.mult x : [0, ∞]) is measurable: R.mult is measurable into ℕ, and every map out of ℕ is measurable (measurable_from_nat). M = R.carrier is measurable (R.measurableSet_carrier), and R.mult x > 0 for x ∈ M (R.mult_pos).
 By definition μ = (Hⁿ⌞M).withDensity θ. Since B is measurable, restriction commutes with taking a density (restrict_withDensity): μ⌞B = ((Hⁿ⌞M)⌞B).withDensity θ.
2. (Translate the hypothesis.) θ is measurable, so ae_withDensity_iff turns the hypothesis 'for μ-a.e. x, x ∈ B → R.mult x = 1' into: for Hⁿ⌞M-a.e. x, θ(x) ≠ 0 → (x ∈ B → R.mult x = 1). Also Hⁿ⌞M-a.e. x lies in M (ae_restrict_mem).
3. (θ = 1 a.e. on B.) Statements holding a.e. for Hⁿ⌞M also hold a.e. for (Hⁿ⌞M)⌞B (ae_restrict_of_ae). Since B is measurable, (Hⁿ⌞M)⌞B-a.e. x lies in B (ae_restrict_mem).
 So for (Hⁿ⌞M)⌞B-a.e. x: x ∈ M, x ∈ B, and the implication of step 2 holds. For such x, R.mult x ≥ 1, so θ(x) ≠ 0. The implication then gives R.mult x = 1, i.e. θ(x) = 1.
 This is the parent's remark that the exceptional set N is Hⁿ-null because θ ≥ 1 on M.
4. (Measure inequality.) By step 3, θ = 1 a.e. for (Hⁿ⌞M)⌞B. Hence ((Hⁿ⌞M)⌞B).withDensity θ = ((Hⁿ⌞M)⌞B).withDensity 1 = (Hⁿ⌞M)⌞B (withDensity_congr_ae, withDensity_one).
 Since B is measurable, (Hⁿ⌞M)⌞B = Hⁿ⌞(B ∩ M) (Measure.restrict_restrict). This is ≤ Hⁿ⌞B because B ∩ M ⊆ B (Measure.restrict_mono).
 With step 1 this gives μ⌞B ≤ Hⁿ⌞B, the first conclusion.
5. (Integral inequality.) Let A ⊆ B and h ≥ 0 be arbitrary. Since A ⊆ B, μ⌞A = (μ⌞B)⌞A and Hⁿ⌞A = (Hⁿ⌞B)⌞A (Measure.restrict_restrict_of_subset). Restriction to A is monotone in the measure (Measure.restrict_mono), so step 4 gives μ⌞A ≤ Hⁿ⌞A.
 The lower integral is monotone in the measure without any measurability hypothesis (lintegral_mono' with h ≤ h). Hence ∫⁻_A h dμ ≤ ∫⁻_A h dHⁿ. ∎
proof_key_steps: θ = R.mult is measurable, θ ≥ 1 on the measurable carrier M, and μ⌞B = ((Hⁿ⌞M)⌞B).withDensity θ for measurable B.
ae_withDensity_iff plus θ ≠ 0 on M turns 'θ = 1 μ-a.e. on B' into θ = 1 (Hⁿ⌞M)⌞B-a.e.
For A ⊆ B, restrict both sides to A and use lintegral_mono' to get ∫⁻_A h dμ ≤ ∫⁻_A h dHⁿ.

audit.reason: The prose and exact proposition agree, including arbitrary A and nonmeasurable h. Measurability and positivity of multiplicity on the carrier justify transferring the almost-everywhere hypothesis through withDensity. Restriction to measurable B then gives density one and measure domination. Restriction monotonicity and lower-integral monotonicity establish the second conclusion without additional measurability or finiteness assumptions. The supplied proof is complete and independent of the parent.

subproblem.title: Frame, dimension and pointwise distance bounds for the affine graph plane
subproblem.statement: Let n, k ∈ ℕ, T an n-dimensional linear subspace of ℝ^{n+k} (Module.finrank ℝ T = n), ι : ℝⁿ → ℝ^{n+k} and ι' : ℝᵏ → ℝ^{n+k} linear isometries with ⟨ιv, ι'w⟩ = 0 and ιv ∈ T for all v ∈ ℝⁿ, w ∈ ℝᵏ, Λ : ℝⁿ → ℝᵏ continuous linear (operator norm ‖Λ‖), ξ ∈ ℝ^{n+k} and c ∈ ℝᵏ. Put τ := ξ + ι'c, L := ι + ι'∘Λ (Lean ι.toLinearMap + ι'.toLinearMap ∘ₗ Λ.toLinearMap), S := LinearMap.range L, and write p_S, p_T for the orthogonal projections onto S and T (Submodule.starProjection). Then: (a) dim S = n (Module.finrank ℝ S = n); (b) for all v ∈ ℝⁿ and w ∈ ℝᵏ, with y := (ξ + ιv + ι'w) − τ: |y − p_S y| ≤ |w − c − Λv| and |v| ≤ |y|; (c) for every x ∈ ℝ^{n+k}: |(x − τ) − p_S(x − τ)| ≤ |(x − ξ) − p_T(x − ξ)| + |c| + ‖Λ‖·|x − τ|.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (n k : ℕ) (T : Submodule ℝ (Euclid (n + k))) (ι : Euclid n →ₗᵢ[ℝ] Euclid (n + k)) (ι' : Euclid k →ₗᵢ[ℝ] Euclid (n + k)) (Λ : Euclid n →L[ℝ] Euclid k) (ξ : Euclid (n + k)) (c : Euclid k), Module.finrank ℝ T = n → (∀ v w, inner ℝ (ι v) (ι' w) = 0) → (∀ v, ι v ∈ T) → Module.finrank ℝ (LinearMap.range (ι.toLinearMap + ι'.toLinearMap ∘ₗ Λ.toLinearMap)) = n ∧ (∀ (v : Euclid n) (w : Euclid k), ‖(ξ + ι v + ι' w - (ξ + ι' c)) - (LinearMap.range (ι.toLinearMap + ι'.toLinearMap ∘ₗ Λ.toLinearMap)).starProjection (ξ + ι v + ι' w - (ξ + ι' c))‖ ≤ ‖w - c - Λ v‖ ∧ ‖v‖ ≤ ‖ξ + ι v + ι' w - (ξ + ι' c)‖) ∧ ∀ x : Euclid (n + k), ‖(x - (ξ + ι' c)) - (LinearMap.range (ι.toLinearMap + ι'.toLinearMap ∘ₗ Λ.toLinearMap)).starProjection (x - (ξ + ι' c))‖ ≤ ‖(x - ξ) - T.starProjection (x - ξ)‖ + ‖c‖ + ‖Λ‖ * ‖x - (ξ + ι' c)‖
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Steps 0–4 of the parent proof of dorag_tes_graph_affine_height. These formalize Simon, Ch. 5, proof of Theorem 4.5 (Tilt-excess Decay Theorem), book/chapter-05.txt lines 960–962: dist(x, τ + S) ≤ |f(x′) − λ(x′)| for x = (x′, f(x′)) ∈ B_{θρ}(τ) ∩ graph f. They also formalize the bound off graph f, which line 967 obtains from the height bound (2) (line 789) and (18) (line 943). Here the frame ℝ^{n+k} = range ι ⊕ range ι′, dim S = n, and these distance bounds are stated without the measure, the Lipschitz map f or the radius t.
1. (Pythagoras.) For v ∈ ℝⁿ and u ∈ ℝᵏ: |ιv + ι'u|² = |ιv|² + 2⟨ιv, ι'u⟩ + |ι'u|² = |v|² + |u|² (norm_add_sq_real). This uses ⟨ιv, ι'u⟩ = 0 and that ι, ι' preserve norms.
2. (Proof of (a).) For w ∈ ℝⁿ, Lw = ιw + ι'(Λw). If Lw = 0, step 1 gives 0 = |Lw|² = |w|² + |Λw|² ≥ |w|², so w = 0. Thus ker L = 0 and L is injective. Hence dim S = dim range L = dim ℝⁿ = n (LinearMap.finrank_range_of_inj, finrank_euclideanSpace_fin).
3. (Nearest point.) For y ∈ ℝ^{n+k} and s ∈ S: |y − p_S y| ≤ |y − s|. Indeed |y − p_S y| = inf_{s' ∈ S}|y − s'| (Submodule.starProjection_minimal). That family of norms is bounded below by 0, so the infimum is at most its value at s (ciInf_le).
4. (Proof of (b).) Fix v ∈ ℝⁿ and w ∈ ℝᵏ. Since ξ cancels and ι' is linear, y = ξ + ιv + ι'w − (ξ + ι'c) = ιv + ι'(w − c).
 The vector s := Lv = ιv + ι'(Λv) lies in S. Also y − s = ι'(w − c) − ι'(Λv) = ι'(w − c − Λv), which has norm |w − c − Λv| because ι' is an isometry. By step 3, |y − p_S y| ≤ |w − c − Λv|.
 By step 1 with u := w − c, |y|² = |v|² + |w − c|² ≥ |v|². Both norms are nonnegative, so |v| ≤ |y|.
5. (range ι = T.) ι is an isometry, hence injective, so dim range ι = dim ℝⁿ = n = dim T. Also range ι ⊆ T by hypothesis. A subspace of the finite-dimensional space T with the same dimension equals T (Submodule.eq_of_le_of_finrank_eq). Hence range ι = T.
6. (range ι' = T^⊥.) Take w ∈ ℝᵏ and u ∈ T. By step 5, u = ιv for some v, so ⟨u, ι'w⟩ = ⟨ιv, ι'w⟩ = 0. Thus ι'w ∈ T^⊥ (Submodule.mem_orthogonal), i.e. range ι' ⊆ T^⊥.
 Next, dim T + dim T^⊥ = dim ℝ^{n+k} = n + k (Submodule.finrank_add_finrank_orthogonal), so dim T^⊥ = k. Since ι' is injective, dim range ι' = k. Hence range ι' = T^⊥ (Submodule.eq_of_le_of_finrank_eq).
7. (Proof of (c).) Fix x ∈ ℝ^{n+k} and put y₀ := x − ξ.
 Since p_T y₀ ∈ T = range ι (step 5), p_T y₀ = ιv for some v ∈ ℝⁿ.
 Since y₀ − p_T y₀ ∈ T^⊥ (Submodule.sub_starProjection_mem_orthogonal) and T^⊥ = range ι' (step 6), y₀ − p_T y₀ = ι'w for some w ∈ ℝᵏ. Moreover |w| = |ι'w| = |(x − ξ) − p_T(x − ξ)|.
 Then x = ξ + p_T y₀ + (y₀ − p_T y₀) = ξ + ιv + ι'w. So (b), applied to this v and w, reads: |(x − τ) − p_S(x − τ)| ≤ |w − c − Λv| and |v| ≤ |x − τ|.
 By the triangle inequality and |Λv| ≤ ‖Λ‖|v| (ContinuousLinearMap.le_opNorm): |w − c − Λv| ≤ |w − c| + |Λv| ≤ |w| + |c| + ‖Λ‖|v|. Since ‖Λ‖ ≥ 0 and |v| ≤ |x − τ|, this is ≤ |w| + |c| + ‖Λ‖|x − τ|.
 Substituting |w| = |(x − ξ) − p_T(x − ξ)| gives (c). Together with steps 2 and 4 this proves (a), (b) and (c). ∎
proof_key_steps: Pythagoras: |ιv + ι'u|² = |v|² + |u|² by orthogonality and the isometry property.
L = ι + ι'∘Λ has |Lw|² ≥ |w|², so it is injective and dim S = n.
Nearest point: |y − p_S y| ≤ |y − s| for every s ∈ S (starProjection_minimal).
(b): y = ιv + ι'(w − c) and y − Lv = ι'(w − c − Λv), so |y − p_S y| ≤ |w − c − Λv|; Pythagoras gives |v| ≤ |y|.
Dimension count: range ι = T and range ι' = T^⊥.
(c): write x − ξ = ιv + ι'w with |w| = |(x − ξ) − p_T(x − ξ)|, apply (b), then the triangle and operator-norm inequalities with |v| ≤ |x − τ|.

audit.reason: The prose and one-line proposition match all hypotheses and three conclusions, including zero-dimensional cases. Pythagoras proves injectivity, dimension and the coordinate bound; projection minimality proves the graph-distance bound. Equal-dimension inclusions identify both frame ranges, allowing the orthogonal decomposition and operator-norm estimate to prove the final bound. Every step is supplied and non-circular. Finite-dimensional projection instances elaborate correctly.

subproblem.title: Area-weight bound for 1-Lipschitz graphs and closed-to-open parameter ball
subproblem.statement: Let n ≥ 1, k ∈ ℕ, f : ℝⁿ → ℝᵏ with |f(v) − f(w)| ≤ |v − w| for all v, w, G : ℝⁿ → [0, ∞] any function and t ∈ ℝ. Then ∫⁻_{B̄ⁿ_t(0)} ofReal(1 + 2ⁿ Σ_{i∈Fin n} |Df(v)e_i|²)·G(v) dv ≤ ofReal(1 + n·2ⁿ)·∫⁻_{B̆ⁿ_t(0)} G(v) dv. Here B̄ⁿ_t(0) = closedBall 0 t and B̆ⁿ_t(0) = ball 0 t (open) in ℝⁿ, dv is Lebesgue measure (volume) on ℝⁿ, Df(v) = fderiv ℝ f v (0 where f is not differentiable), e_i = EuclideanSpace.single i 1, both sides are lower integrals, and the constant ofReal(1 + n·2ⁿ) multiplies the whole open-ball integral.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (n k : ℕ), 0 < n → ∀ (f : Euclid n → Euclid k), (∀ v w, ‖f v - f w‖ ≤ ‖v - w‖) → ∀ (G : Euclid n → ℝ≥0∞) (t : ℝ), (∫⁻ v in closedBall (0 : Euclid n) t, ENNReal.ofReal (1 + 2 ^ n * ∑ i : Fin n, ‖fderiv ℝ f v (EuclideanSpace.single i (1 : ℝ))‖ ^ 2) * G v) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (1 + n * 2 ^ n) * (∫⁻ v in ball (0 : Euclid n) t, G v)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Step 6.2 (second half) and Step 6.3 of the parent proof of dorag_tes_graph_affine_height. Step 6.2's second half is the weight bound Σ_i|Df(v)e_i|² ≤ n for 1-Lipschitz f, followed by lintegral_const_mul; Step 6.3 says the sphere is Lⁿ-null, so closed and open parameter balls give equal lower integrals. Together they formalize the area-formula comparison in Simon, Ch. 5, proof of Theorem 4.5, book/chapter-05.txt: the graph integral at lines 963–965 is compared with the parameter integral (19) at line 949, using Lip f ≤ 1 from (3) at line 795. Here they are stated for an arbitrary integrand G.
1. (Derivative bound.) The hypothesis says dist(f v, f w) ≤ 1·dist(v, w), so f is 1-Lipschitz (LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul). Hence ‖Df(v)‖ ≤ 1 for every v ∈ ℝⁿ (norm_fderiv_le_of_lipschitz). This holds also where f is not differentiable, since there Df(v) = 0.
2. (Sum bound.) For each i ∈ Fin n, |e_i| = 1, so |Df(v)e_i| ≤ ‖Df(v)‖·|e_i| = ‖Df(v)‖ ≤ 1 (ContinuousLinearMap.le_opNorm). Since 0 ≤ |Df(v)e_i| ≤ 1, we get |Df(v)e_i|² ≤ 1. Summing over the n indices gives Σ_{i∈Fin n}|Df(v)e_i|² ≤ n.
3. (Weight bound.) Since 2ⁿ ≥ 0, step 2 gives 1 + 2ⁿΣ_i|Df(v)e_i|² ≤ 1 + n·2ⁿ. ENNReal.ofReal is monotone, so ofReal(1 + 2ⁿΣ_i|Df(v)e_i|²) ≤ ofReal(1 + n·2ⁿ) for every v.
4. (Pull out the constant.) Multiplying step 3 by G(v) ≥ 0 and using pointwise monotonicity of the lower integral (lintegral_mono, no measurability needed): LHS ≤ ∫⁻_{B̄ⁿ_t(0)} ofReal(1 + n·2ⁿ)·G(v) dv. Since ofReal(1 + n·2ⁿ) ≠ ∞, lintegral_const_mul' turns this into ofReal(1 + n·2ⁿ)·∫⁻_{B̄ⁿ_t(0)} G(v) dv.
5. (Closed vs open ball.) Since n ≥ 1, Fin n is nonempty, so ℝⁿ is nontrivial. Lebesgue measure on ℝⁿ is an additive Haar measure, so every sphere sphere 0 t is null, for every t ∈ ℝ (Measure.addHaar_sphere).
 Also closedBall 0 t ∖ ball 0 t = sphere 0 t, and ball 0 t ∖ closedBall 0 t = ∅ because ball ⊆ closedBall. Hence closedBall 0 t = ball 0 t almost everywhere (ae_eq_set), and the lower integrals of G over the two sets coincide (setLIntegral_congr).
6. Combining steps 4 and 5: LHS ≤ ofReal(1 + n·2ⁿ)·∫⁻_{B̆ⁿ_t(0)} G(v) dv. ∎
proof_key_steps: f is 1-Lipschitz, so ‖Df(v)‖ ≤ 1 everywhere (norm_fderiv_le_of_lipschitz; Df = 0 off differentiability).
|Df(v)e_i| ≤ 1 for each i, so Σ_i|Df(v)e_i|² ≤ n and the weight is ≤ ofReal(1 + n·2ⁿ).
lintegral_mono, then lintegral_const_mul' (the constant is finite), pulls the constant out of the closed-ball integral.
For n ≥ 1 the sphere is Lebesgue-null (addHaar_sphere), so closedBall 0 t =ᵐ ball 0 t and the integrals agree (setLIntegral_congr).

audit.reason: The one-line proposition exactly matches the stated weight, coefficient, volume measure and integral scopes. The global derivative-norm bound applies also at nondifferentiability points; unit basis vectors give the sum bound. Finite constant extraction is valid for arbitrary G. Positive n ensures a nontrivial Euclidean space, so sphere nullity identifies closed- and open-ball restrictions for every real radius, including zero and negative radii. The supplied proof is complete and non-circular.
